chapter: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
title: How little records mattered to bands and bookings
summary: Records were unpopular until Armstrong's Hot Five; Mamie Smith and Johnny Dunn sold best, and recording paid little and did not bring bookings.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Now, records, how important were records to a band, for instance?

Well they weren't too popular in those days. Recording was just -- it was hard to get a recording, because they weren't buying records in those days, other than say Mame Smith records. Mame Smith I think sold more records than any of the singers. During that time. I think before Bessie, maybe.

Sold more records than any of them. And until Louie started recording with his Hot Five. Now after he started, then records sales started going up. Then other groups started recording, also. Jimmy Noon sold a lot of records too. But not as many as Armstrong did. Cause records weren't too popular. Not jazz records, not until that time. Of course, Johnny Dunn, he sold -- he was I think -- he was the first jazz hit record recording. That I know about.
But records -- lot of performers didn't get paid a lot of money for making records?
Oh, no, you didn't get paid very much.
I was wondering whether they looked on the records as sales tools, in other words if you had a recording out, didn't that increase that -- your chance of

getting good bookings? I don't think so. I really don't think so. Now of course Fletcher Henderson had a lot of recordings, then. They're -- weren't too many of them bought. They didn't sell too many of them. I don't think they had anything to do with it at all, not like today. Records didn't mean that much to --
